clue.text: Fashion company is a gold mine. — hence the enigmatic expression!

indicators.note: to fashion something is to shape it anew, so the letters given are worked into a fresh order

parts.note: taken letter for letter as part of the mix

explanation.surface: A fashion house is making a fortune, which explains someone's knowing little smile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fashion' poses as a noun but is the anagram signal, working on CO plus ISAGOLDMINE. La Gioconda is the Italian name for the Mona Lisa, famous for her mysterious smile.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonardo's Mona Lisa, known in Italy as La Gioconda, wears a famously inscrutable smile.

clue.text: Start of the high road to Scotland by the biggest builders

definitions.text: Start of the high road to Scotland by the biggest builders

parts.words: Start of the high road to Scotland by the biggest builders
parts.note: legend says the giant Finn McCool built a stone road across the sea from Antrim towards Scotland; the basalt columns are its surviving start

explanation.surface: A road-building firm begins a grand highway north to Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'biggest builders' are giants, not construction firms: the clue describes the Antrim coast's basalt rock formation, said in legend to be the start of a giant's road to Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: The Northern Irish basalt formation is, in folklore, a stepping-stone road begun by a giant heading for Scotland.

clue.text: Smell nothing from one end of the river to the other

indicators.note: this phrase, completed by 'to the other', tells us a letter shifts from one end of the river's name
completes the instruction: the shifted letter lands at the opposite end of the river's name

parts.note: the Douro is the river flowing through Spain and Portugal to Porto
nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: Along the whole length of a river there is no smell at all.
explanation.walkthrough: The Douro is the Iberian river of port wine fame. Moving its final O (nothing) to the front gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A smell is a scent or whiff, whether pleasant or not.

clue.text: About-time the great one in the race got ready

annotationWithheld.why: About time the great one in the race got ready (2,3,5): ON (about) + T (time) leaves HEALERT, and no reading of 'the great one in the race' gives those letters; the scan prints the same clue and no search finds a parse
annotationWithheld.clue: About-time the great one in the race got ready

clue.text: Stoker's blood count recorded in book:

definitions.text: Stoker's blood count recorded in book

parts.words: Stoker's blood count recorded in book
parts.note: Bram Stoker wrote a novel about a blood-drinking Transylvanian nobleman; 'blood count' reads as a medical test but means that aristocrat

explanation.surface: A stoker's blood test result is written up in a medical record.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stoker' looks like a man feeding a furnace and 'blood count' a medical test; really it is Bram Stoker and his vampire nobleman, title of his 1897 novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Bram Stoker's 1897 novel is named after its vampire nobleman, a count who drinks blood.

clue.text: Sort of coin — shilling

parts.note: specie is money in coin rather than notes
S is the abbreviation for a shilling, the old British coin worth twelve pence

explanation.surface: Some kind of coin, namely a shilling.
explanation.walkthrough: A shilling was a pre-1971 British coin; it was abbreviated s, as in the old £sd.
explanation.definitionFit: A sort is a kind or type, and a species is a kind of thing.

clue.text: Black in American state

parts.note: taken as written
KY is the postal abbreviation for Kentucky

explanation.surface: Someone blackballed somewhere in the United States.
explanation.definitionFit: Ink is typically dark, so something stained or coloured like ink is black.

clue.text: Ecology leader railing about dis -ease from the outflow

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter, here of Ecology
the railing is placed round the illness, so it goes about it

parts.note: a fence is a railing
flu is a disease; the printed word is broken by a line-end hyphen

explanation.surface: A green campaigner rails against the illness caused by sewage discharge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'railing' looks like ranting, but it is FENCE, which goes 'about' FLU; E comes first, from the leader of 'Ecology'.
explanation.definitionFit: A discharge or flowing out of liquid, such as waste water, is an outflow.

clue.text: These figures are not classical — see the square corners

definitions.text: These figures are not classical — see the square corners

parts.words: These figures are not classical — see the square corners
parts.note: the classical number system is the Roman one; the other set of digits is said to have been drawn with a count of angles, hence the corners

explanation.surface: A remark on modern statues, not classical ones, with their squared-off edges.
explanation.walkthrough: 'figures' suggests statues, but means numerals. A popular story claims each digit was first drawn with as many angles as its value.
explanation.definitionFit: The everyday digits 0 to 9 came to Europe through Arab scholars, unlike the classical Roman system.

clue.text: Look the other way in a boxing match with effrontery

parts.note: a bout is a boxing contest
face means cheek or nerve, as in 'having the face to ask'

explanation.surface: Turning away in a prize fight shows a lot of cheek.
explanation.definitionFit: To turn right round on the spot is to reverse direction and so face the other way.

clue.text: African king, almost fiery

parts.note: K is the chess abbreviation for king

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the synonym for fiery is cut short

parts.note: afire means burning, fiery

explanation.surface: An African monarch with a hot temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' drops the last letter of AFIRE. The answer is a dated term, now offensive in South Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: Historically a name for a member of a southern African Bantu-speaking people; now a slur and not used.

clue.text: Cast reported fit here

indicators.note: reported means spoken of, so the synonym for cast is taken as heard

parts.note: to cast is to throw

explanation.surface: An actor company said to be suitable for this venue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast' looks like the actors in a play but is the verb, to throw. 'here' merely links.
explanation.definitionFit: A pang or spasm, a sudden fit of pain, as in the agonies of childbirth.

clue.text: One piece of furniture

explanation.surface: A single item of furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: A single thing counts as one; a fitted cupboard or kitchen module is a piece of furniture.

clue.text: Underground source of a flower.

parts.note: plants such as tulips grow from a swollen buried storage organ; 'Underground' seems to suggest the Tube or secrecy

explanation.surface: A hidden supplier of blooms.
explanation.walkthrough: Daffodils and tulips grow each year from a rounded store of food buried in the soil.
explanation.definitionFit: A rounded storage organ in the soil from which a tulip or daffodil grows.

clue.text: Second XI tense, not wasting any energy

parts.note: eleven players make a team, as in a cricket or football side
tense means taut, tight

explanation.surface: A reserve side is nervous but conserving their strength.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second XI' reads as a reserve cricket or football side, but splits into S and TEAM.
explanation.definitionFit: A seal that lets no vapour escape loses none of the power held in the steam.

clue.text: This softens the sound of the sea

definitions.text: This softens the sound of the sea

parts.words: This softens the sound of the sea
parts.note: 'the sea' when spoken is the letter C, and a hook under that letter makes it soft, as in French façade

explanation.surface: Something that dampens the roar of the waves.
explanation.walkthrough: The sea's sound is the letter C, said aloud; the small hook placed under C, as in façade, turns its hard K sound into a soft S.
explanation.definitionFit: A diacritic hook placed beneath the letter C to show it is pronounced like S.

clue.text: Dull lampoon that doesn't come off

definitions.text: Dull lampoon that doesn't come off

parts.note: damp means dull, lacking spirit
a squib is a short satirical piece, a lampoon

explanation.surface: A tame satire that falls flat.
explanation.walkthrough: A squib is also a small firework; when damp it fizzles out, hence anything that fails to impress.
explanation.definitionFit: A wet firework fizzles instead of exploding, so the phrase names any letdown that fails to impress.

clue.text: Diabolical acts in a revolution

indicators.note: a revolution turns things over, so the letters of acts in a are overturned into new order

explanation.surface: Wicked deeds carried out during an uprising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolution' suggests a political rising but signals an anagram of ACTSINA.
explanation.definitionFit: Devilish, belonging to or like the Devil.

clue.text: Not to do with behaviour in a French lesson

parts.note: UN is French for a
a moral is the lesson of a story

explanation.surface: Something irrelevant to conduct comes up in a French class.
explanation.definitionFit: Outside the scope of ethics altogether, neither good nor bad in conduct.

clue.text: Animal accommodation for a pound

explanation.surface: Where livestock are kept, a holding pen.
explanation.walkthrough: A pound is an enclosure for stray or impounded animals, not money or weight.
explanation.definitionFit: Pens where cattle rest at a market or abattoir; a pound is likewise an enclosure for stock.

clue.text: Top flat in a high-rise?

parts.note: 'Top flat' suggests a penthouse apartment, but means a level summit on raised ground

explanation.surface: An apartment on the uppermost floor of a tower block.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top flat' and 'high-rise' paint an apartment block; read again, it is level ground on top of an elevated area.
explanation.definitionFit: An area of level high land, flat on top though raised up.

clue.text: Greedy person on the end in the queue

parts.note: a glutton is called a pig
a tail is the end of something

explanation.surface: A glutton waiting at the back of the line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'queue' suggests a line of people, but an old sense is a plait of hair hanging down the back.
explanation.definitionFit: Queue is an old word for a plait of hair worn hanging at the back of the head.

clue.text: A piece of cake, readily obtainable

explanation.surface: A slice of cake that is easy to come by.
explanation.definitionFit: A piece of cake is slang for something simple; goods that are readily obtainable are freely available.

clue.text: Pinion a flapper

explanation.surface: Tying up a 1920s party girl.
explanation.walkthrough: A flapper is a 1920s fashionable young woman, but here it is anything that flaps.
explanation.definitionFit: To pinion is to wound or clip a bird's limb used for flight; a bird flaps that limb.

clue.text: Nearly a bull's-eye got the shield

indicators.note: nearly means not quite all, so the word for bull's-eye loses its final letter

parts.note: the bull's-eye is the target aimed at

explanation.surface: An archer almost hits the bull's-eye but strikes a shield instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A small round shield of the kind carried by Highland soldiers.

clue.text: He is getting up to source of river in Hohenlinden

indicators.note: the source of a river is where it starts, so take the word's opening letter

parts.note: Thomas Campbell's poem Hohenlinden names the river Iser, rolling rapidly past the battlefield

explanation.surface: A man climbing towards the headwaters of a Bavarian river.
explanation.walkthrough: Campbell's poem Hohenlinden, about an 1800 battle in Bavaria, names the river as the Iser (now usually Isar).
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who gets out of bed, as in an early bird, is so called.

clue.text: Tumbled to the Moor

explanation.surface: Someone fell over on the moor.
explanation.walkthrough: In northern England a moorland hill is called by this word, as in the Lake District.
explanation.definitionFit: Tumbled means dropped down; in northern England a stretch of upland moor is so called.

clue.text: Damage in a bus engine

indicators.note: in tells us the answer lies inside the words a bus engine

explanation.surface: Wear and tear inside a bus's motor.
explanation.definitionFit: Misuse or ill-treatment that harms something.

clue.text: For sale again, new formula pain relief

indicators.note: a new formula is a reworking, so the letters of sale again are made up afresh

explanation.surface: A painkiller relaunched in a new formulation and put back on sale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new formula' suggests a drug's recipe, but signals rearranging SALEAGAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Absence of feeling of pain, the effect a painkiller produces.

clue.text: Literary bits a hindrance in best seller, perhaps

indicators.note: in says the hindrance goes within the rearranged letters
perhaps suggests the letters of best seller may be in another order

parts.note: a let is a hindrance, as in 'without let or hindrance', and in tennis

explanation.surface: Fine writing gets in the way of a popular novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges BESTSELLER and LET goes 'in' it. The French term means fine writing, essays and literary works.
explanation.definitionFit: Elegant literary writing, essays and criticism rather than practical prose.
